p:BIH: The convertible mark is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are put into circulation only against convertible foreign currency the bank holds, at 1.95583 marks to the euro, and its monetary liabilities may never exceed its foreign currency assets. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it has joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training and asset management, with the announcement stating the membership rather than which of those services the bank takes. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 for independence, 11th of 155 countries, and no government pressure was reported in the quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is documented: in 2023 a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softic of suspected wrongdoing in several matters, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The prosecutor's office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations, which remain unproven, while the bank said examining allegations is not an investigation and that reports of one were untrue. Grant Thornton d.o.o. Banja Luka audited the 2016 accounts. The bank holds 3.5 tonnes of gold and scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One career move is recorded. The Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina's own profile page gives Jasmina Selimovic's dated career: at the Faculty of Economics in Sarajevo since 2004, its Dean from 2018 and renewed in 2022; in the Fiscal Council's advisory group from 2011 to 2015; an independent member of the Supervisory Board of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2018; president of the board of the Sarajevo Canton Institute of Health Insurance since 2021; and a member of the bank's Governing Board from 3 January 2024. The central bank's page leaves the ownership of Raiffeisen Bank Bosnia and Herzegovina unstated; that bank's own ownership page lists Raiffeisen SEE Region Holding GmbH as sole owner at 100 per cent, with no state shareholder, which is what makes this a move involving a private bank. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. Its notes are printed abroad, by three firms in turn. The bank contracted the French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire to print 100-denar notes, reported on 8 May 2026, for 59,800,000 denars, about 972,358 euros. It had contracted the Russian state company Goznak for the 100-denar notes in 2021, for about 400,000 euros, as part of a 2.2 million euro reissue carrying the state's changed constitutional name. Three separate contracts with De La Rue International cover the 10, 500 and 1,000 denar notes, 45 million notes for 3.775 million euros in total, 20 million of them polymer. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. The European Central Bank gave the bank a temporary line to borrow euros against collateral from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024, which has expired. One career move is on record and it too stays outside the private sector, so it is listed but not counted: governor Anita Angelovska Bezhoska spent about eight years at the Ministry of Finance, ending as manager of the treasury department, and was state secretary in 2003 and 2004, then worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund in Washington before joining the bank as chief economist, serving almost eight years as vice-governor and becoming governor in May 2018. The page the bank publishes names no private firm and no commercial bank. Its books are checked from outside by Grant Thornton DOO of Skopje, which signed the independent auditor's report on the bank's 2023 financial statements and gave an opinion without qualifications; the bank publishes that report on its own site and in the Official Gazette.
p:TJK: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series. Its books are checked from outside by RSM Tajikistan LLC of Dushanbe, whose managing partner signed the independent auditor's report on the 2023 financial statements. Worth noticing is that the firm holds a licence to audit banks issued by the National Bank itself, so the body being audited also licenses its auditor. Earlier audits were done by Deloitte and by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder.
p:PAK: The State Bank of Pakistan is the country's central bank. It scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case from 2025 is alleged and unproven. In August 2025 Pakistan Observer reported, citing internal memos and cash slips, that senior officials including an executive director issued bulk fresh banknotes directly to private brokers, who resold them at premiums, with each transaction netting officials at least 2 million rupees in kickbacks. It said no probe had been opened. The state has also turned its own auditors on the bank: on 8 August 2023 the National Assembly's Public Accounts Committee, chaired by Noor Alam Khan, directed the Auditor General to audit the State Bank over the disbursement of about 1,145 billion rupees in TERF concessional loans, and directed an inquiry into whether those loans went out on merit. In January 2014 governor Yaseen Anwar resigned; the Finance Ministry spokesman said he cited personal reasons, while unnamed senior officials said it covered differences with Finance Minister Ishaq Dar over inflation and reserves. Anwar had come to the bank from private finance, and the bank's own profile of him gives the dates: he trained at JPMorgan Chase in New York from 1973 to 1975, spent about fifteen years at Bank of America from 1976 to 1991 ending as a vice president in its global export finance group, was a vice president at Merrill Lynch in New York and London from 1992 to 2001, and was a non-executive director of United National Bank Ltd. (U.K.) from 2000 to 2006, before being appointed deputy governor on 29 March 2007 and governor on 19 October 2011. Two governors came from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund: Ishrat Husain, appointed in December 1999, and Reza Baqir, appointed in May 2019 after leading the IMF's Debt Policy Division. KPMG and BDO audit its accounts.
p:KHM: The National Bank of Cambodia is the country's central bank. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and neither matter on record was ever confirmed. The Phnom Penh Post reported that governor Thor Peng Leath lent three million US dollars of central bank money on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet its minimum capital, which bank officials admitted was highly irregular, and that on 8 May 1995 the bank released 145,000 dollars from former commerce minister Var Huot's frozen account. Preferential treatment was claimed, but Var Huot said there was none, and no charges or findings followed. In November 2013 Chea Serey, daughter of governor Chea Chanto, was promoted to director-general; former deputy governor Tioulong Saumura said being the governor's daughter should exclude her, Nguon Sokha called her a skilled technocrat, and no investigation followed. Who holds the bank's leadership is set out in its founding law and has no end date. Under the Law on the Organization and Conduct of the National Bank of Cambodia of 26 January 1996, the Governor and Deputy Governor are appointed, replaced and dismissed by royal decree on the recommendation of the Royal Government, with that article naming no grounds a dismissal must meet; the other board members are appointed and dismissed by sub-decree; the seven-member board seats both a representative of the Ministry of Economy and Finance and a representative of the head of the Royal Government; and the bank may not withdraw currency from circulation without the Royal Government's consent. Policy itself is set by the board, which the law requires only to consult the government. The riel is made in-house, by the bank's own Banknote Printing Works, which printed the 200,000-riel note issued on 16 October 2024 for the twentieth anniversary of King Norodom Sihamoni's coronation. The bank belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which central banks join for help with their reserves. BNY Mellon supplies it with reporting systems and staff training.
p:BRN: Brunei Darussalam Central Bank issues the Brunei dollar and runs it as a currency board, meaning the dollar is held at a fixed rate against the Singapore dollar. Under an agreement set up in 1967, the Brunei bank and Singapore's monetary authority each take in the other's notes and coins from banks and exchange them at par without charge. The bank has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, through the ASEAN+3 regional scheme, to which Brunei contributes 0.06 billion US dollars against a maximum arrangement of 0.3 billion, though the factsheet says the member is the country, not necessarily the central bank. Note Printing Australia has printed notes for Brunei: the Reserve Bank of Australia's 2007 report lists the Brunei Currency and Monetary Board among that printer's export orders in 2006/07, without giving a number of notes. PricewaterhouseCoopers Services audits the accounts. No case at the bank is documented. Who sits on its board is a matter of record, and it is the government: the bank announced on 21 October 2025 that His Majesty the Sultan had consented to the appointment of its directors, naming the Minister of Primary Resources and Tourism as Chairman and the Deputy Minister of Finance and Economy as Deputy Chairman, with the Deputy State Mufti, two permanent secretaries, the Solicitor General and the bank's own managing director as the other members. The announcement gives no term. This rests on the bank's own announcement rather than on the Central Bank Order of 2010, which it does not publish anywhere a reader can reach. Its law scores 0.704 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 50 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BHR: The Central Bank of Bahrain, created in 1973, issues the Bahraini Dinar (BHD), held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 30 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (56): the country's laws hide who owns money, and financial secrecy scores 69 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.515 of 1 on one index (rank 135 of 155) and 0.433 on another (rank 156 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. The pressure here is built into the law instead, and it has no end date. Under the Central Bank of Bahrain and Financial Institutions Law of 2006, all seven board members, one of them a representative of the Ministry of Finance, hold office by Royal Decree for renewable four-year terms, and that decree names the chairman and vice chairman; the Governor, who has ministerial rank, is appointed by Royal Decree. Article 173 then has the Minister watch whether the bank is keeping to the general economic policy of the Kingdom, and where the Minister sees a conflict and the board holds to its own view, the Minister refers the disagreement to the Cabinet, which settles it by an order issued within thirty days. A swap line, which is an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, runs both ways with the United Arab Emirates: BHD 2 billion (AED 20 billion), signed 8 April 2026, for up to 5 years. De La Rue printed the 20-dinar note. The bank's accounts are audited by KPMG Fakhro of Manama, which signed its report on the 2023 financial statements on 10 March 2024. Rasheed Mohammed Al Maraj has been Governor since January 2005; immediately before joining the bank he was General Manager and Chief Executive Officer of the Arab Petroleum Investments Company, APICORP, in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, and earlier he was Assistant Under-Secretary at Bahrain's Ministry of Finance and National Economy and Under-Secretary at the Ministry of Transportation.
p:OMN: The Central Bank of Oman, created in 1974, issues the Omani rial and holds it at a fixed rate, a peg, to the US dollar as of December 2025. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, with financial secrecy at 72.4 of 100. Independence written into its law scores 0.618 of 1 on one index and 0.46 on another, both measured on the law as it stood before 2025. That law has since been replaced. From 1 January 2025 Royal Decree 2/2025 issued a new Banking Law repealing the one of 2000, and Royal Decree 3/2025 issued the System of the Central Bank of Oman, a twenty-one article statute that serves as the bank's own governing act and is described as giving it legal, financial and administrative independence. The board is nonetheless made by decree: Royal Decree 4/2025 appointed a member of the ruling family as Chairman and made the Minister of Economy Deputy Chairman, with the Governor, the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Finance and the chairman of the Financial Services Authority among the members, and Royal Decree 5/2025 appointed the Governor with the rank of Minister. It holds 6.7 tonnes of gold, 3.6 per cent of reserves. Oman's first polymer note, a 1-rial commemorative reported for introduction on 11 January 2026, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient; that is a commemorative, not the circulating series. Oman scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2023 is signed by KPMG at Muscat on 7 May 2024.
p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post. Prime Minister John Briceno said the board had recommended he resign because of a lot of policy differences. Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance, that he faced opposition from it, and that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy. Castillo Sanchez & Burrell, LLP, Chartered Accountants audited the 2013 accounts, and De La Rue printed the new 100-dollar note introduced on 4 August 2025. Belize scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and it tells the public little, 4 of 15 on a transparency measure in 2019. Two career moves are recorded, both out of the bank and back into it. The Central Bank of Belize's own Office of the Governor page gives Kareem Michael as Monetary Economist in 2000 and Deputy Director of Research in 2008, says he resigned in 2014 to become Senior Business Analyst at Belize Electricity Limited, and records him returning as Deputy Governor in November 2017, Acting Governor on 13 August 2021 and Governor on 1 December 2021. Who owns Belize Electricity Limited is not stated there, and it is a utility rather than a financial firm. The second move does run through private finance, in the bank's own words: the same page says Deputy Governor Marina Laetitia Murillo joined the bank as a research officer in August 1991, worked from 1998 in project management in the non-government sector and in management positions in the private financial sector, and returned in November 2011 as Economist I, becoming assistant manager of the financial system development unit in October 2018 and Deputy Governor on 1 September 2022. The firms are not named. Moving between jobs is not wrongdoing.
p:MNG: The Bank of Mongolia issues the tugrik. Two cases and two departures centre on N. Zoljargal, governor from 2012, who was replaced on 20 July 2016, two years before his term was due to end and with no reason given. The anti-corruption agency IAAC arrested him on 29 November 2017 over the Chinggis bond and a price-stabilising programme, part of a wider look at how the bank was run from 2012 to 2016; a court released him with a travel ban, prosecutors had not formally charged him and no later outcome was found, so nothing there is proven. In April 2020 he and three politicians were reported charged with abuse of power over illegally transferring 49 per cent of the Erdenet Mining Company; no outcome is recorded and those charges are unproven too. Lawmakers accepted the resignation of his successor, Nadmid Bayartsaikhan, on 21 November 2019, after the Financial Action Task Force, which sets international rules against money laundering, put Mongolia on its grey list over enforcement. The present governor, B. Lkhagvasuren, came from the World Bank in Washington to the bank as adviser to the governor in 2000, and the rest of his career is in Mongolian public bodies. Two more careers run between the bank and the banks it supervises. Khosjargal Undraa joined the Supervisory Board in 2025 after thirteen years at Golomt Bank, from branch teller in 2006 to project director of its business process re-engineering project in 2018 and 2019, then deputy director of MIG LLC and chief executive of BPM Mongolia; Golomt's own account of itself says it was set up in 1995 as a subsidiary of Bodi International and became a joint-stock company at its 2022 listing, naming no state shareholder. Enkhjargal Danzanbaljir's career stays inside the public sector and so is listed without being counted: chief economist and adviser to the governor, London representative, Deputy Governor from 2007 to 2010, then the Asian Development Bank, the AIIB, the World Bank, an EU and GIZ project, the intergovernmental International Investment Bank and the state-owned State Bank of Mongolia, before rejoining the Supervisory Board in 2025. Ernst & Young Mongolia Audit LLC audited the accounts for the 2020 financial year, and Giesecke & Devrient printed the new 5,000-togrog note. It holds two currency swap lines with China, arrangements to lend each other money, one renewed on 26 June 2026 at 15 billion yuan against 7.85 trillion tugrik, and scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:ZMB: The Bank of Zambia issues the kwacha, which floats within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Zambia scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its law scores 0.637 of 1 for written independence from government. The bank launched its Heritage Series of six notes and six coins on 31 March 2025, and the 10 and 20 kwacha notes were printed on Landqart's Durasafe composite substrate; the bank thanked Landqart publicly at the launch and was given a frame of unprinted 10 and 20 kwacha notes. Who printed the series is not published: BanknoteNews records the printer as unknown for every denomination. Denny Kalyalya came to the governorship in February 2015 from the World Bank Group, where he had been executive director for the Africa Group One constituency. On 22 August 2020 President Edgar Lungu dismissed him, less than a week after he warned of economic difficulties, and appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry; Kalyalya returned as governor in October 2021. In October 2015 the Drug Enforcement Commission arrested a section officer for theft by a public servant and money laundering, accusing him of taking 43,660 US dollars and 20,335 kwacha in cash between January and September 2015; he was charged, and no court outcome is given, so the accusation is unproven. The Auditor General audits the accounts each year under the Bank of Zambia Act No. 5 of 2022. One career move is on record and it does not run through private finance, so it is listed but not counted: Investrust Bank announced on 16 April 2015 that Dr Richard K. E. Chembe, who had held senior management posts at the Bank of Zambia and the International Monetary Fund, would become its managing director from 1 May 2015, subject to the Bank of Zambia's approval. Investrust is not a private employer in the sense this layer counts: ZCCM Investments Holdings, which describes itself as state owned, raised its stake in it from 45.4 to 71.4 per cent in 2018 and was already its largest shareholder at the time of the appointment.
p:ZWE: The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issues the ZiG, which circulates alongside foreign currency. From 2003 to 2013, under governor Gideon Gono, it ran quasi-fiscal activities, handing out cash and farm equipment at events presided over by President Mugabe and raiding private foreign-currency accounts to fund state operations, leaving debts of close to 1.3 billion dollars that a 2014 government bill moved onto taxpayers. In 2009 the Movement for Democratic Change demanded Gono be replaced, saying Western donors would not fund reconstruction until he went; Mugabe said he would stay, and he was not removed. Gono stepped down in December 2013, and in March 2014 finance minister Patrick Chinamasa, citing President Robert Mugabe, announced the appointment of John Mangudya, then chief executive of the Harare-based commercial bank CBZ, to head the bank from 1 May 2014. At a parliamentary Public Accounts Committee hearing in September 2019, deputy governor Mlambo confirmed the bank had issued 663.8 million US dollars in Treasury Bills in 2017 and 2018 to Sakunda Holdings, owned by presidential ally Kudakwashe Tagwirei, on Finance Ministry instruction; the committee also cited a 1.37 billion dollar overdraft issued without parliamentary approval. Both matters stand as official findings. Government pressure was reported in 8 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, always to ease policy. The country's notes are made by a company the bank itself owns: Fidelity Printers and Refiners of Harare, whose own corporate history says it began printing secure banknotes in 1966 in the basement of the old Reserve Bank building on Samora Machel Avenue and moved to purpose-built premises at Msasa in 1978-82. In 2021 the printing side was split off into a separate company, the Printing and Minting Company of Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BMU: Bermuda's money is the Bermudian dollar, issued by the Bermuda Monetary Authority, which is the central bank. As of December 2025 the dollar sat in a de facto peg to the US dollar, meaning it is held at a fixed rate in practice. Bermuda scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 50, mainly because the island's laws hide who owns money: financial secrecy is 71.3 of 100, 54th of 141 places, while the World Bank's measure of control of corruption puts it at 72 of 100. Independence written into law is almost absent, 0.06 of 1 and second from last of 191 places, with no reform since 1970, and the bank scores 3.5 of 15 for what it tells the public. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The Office of the Auditor-General audits the accounts, as it did for 2021. The notes are printed abroad: the authority announced on 30 October 2024 that its new 2 and 5 dollar notes, printed by De La Rue on polymer, would enter circulation that autumn, Bermuda's first polymer notes and among the first anywhere to carry King Charles III's effigy.
p:TKM: The Central Bank of Turkmenistan issues the manat. Its law leaves most of the power with the government: 0.41 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and 0.183 on another, ranking it 187 of 191. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, the largest part being corruption and secrecy around it, at 74. In March 2002 the prosecutor's office accused former central bank chairman Orazov of embezzling 120 million US dollars in German and Swiss loans. On 29 December 2002 the Supreme Court sentenced Orazov in absentia to 25 years over alleged involvement in the armed attack on President Niyazov of 25 November 2002, and the People's Council raised that to life imprisonment the next day; Amnesty International called the trial grossly unfair. That conviction is for the alleged attack, not the loan accusation, which remains unproven. In January 2014 President Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov dismissed the bank's head, Tuvakmammet Japarov, for unspecified flaws in his work. Its notes are printed abroad by De La Rue, which printed the commemorative 200-manat polymer note introduced on 1 December 2025 for the thirtieth anniversary of permanent neutrality.
p:YEM: The Central Bank of Yemen issues the rial, held close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the corruption and secrecy around it stand at 86. Government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for easier money or for printing money. On 18 September 2016 President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, announcing from Saudi Arabia, sacked central bank head Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden, with no official reason given. On 6 December 2021 he dismissed the governor and his deputy, the fourth such sacking since the civil war began. A UN Panel of Experts report in January 2021 said the Aden-based bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered 'a substantial part' of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims, and on 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations. Its money is printed in Russia. The Russian foreign ministry confirmed in June 2020 that the state printer Goznak had been printing notes for Yemen's government under a commercial contract signed in 2017, after separatists in Aden seized a convoy carrying 64 billion rials, about 255 million US dollars, of Russian-printed banknotes.
p:ERI: The Bank of Eritrea issues the currency (ERN). Eritrea scores 52 of 100 on exposure (0 means shielded from outside influence, 100 means fully exposed), rank 7 of 194, more exposed than 96% of the 194 places with a figure. Outside influence scores 19 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 86, the weakest side, mainly from corruption in the country. The Corruption Perceptions Index is 13 of 100 (clean rank 177 of 182) and World Bank control of corruption is 16 of 100. No documented case at the central bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Who prints the nakfa is recorded only weakly: an encyclopaedia entry says the current series is printed by the German firm Giesecke+Devrient, and no document from the Bank of Eritrea confirming it was found, so that rests on the encyclopaedia alone. The country has had 1 systemic banking crisis since 1970. On the Cukierman method for independence written into law, the bank scores 0.423 of 1 (rank 160 of 191, 2023). It was created in 1993 and has had 2 reforms since 1970, both raising independence. In December 2025 the exchange rate was a dual market with parallel-market data missing, and no anchor was found. Gold holdings are 0 tonnes, 0% of reserves (117 of 122).
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury for advice on managing reserves. Who prints the ouguiya is not published, but part of what it is printed on is: the 50-ouguiya note marking fifty years of the currency, introduced on 18 June 2023, was issued on three different substrates, Durasafe composite by Landqart, paper with sisal by Oberthur and Hybrid by Louisenthal, while the printer itself is recorded as unknown. A substrate maker is not a printer, so Mauritania still has no printer on record. Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the Central Bank of Mauritania, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single relayed account by IRIN, so it is a claim, not confirmed.
p:MDV: The Maldives Monetary Authority issues the Maldivian rufiyaa, and its record turns on one scandal: the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the authority negligent. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that watches for suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF but did not look into it properly, did not examine SOF's large transactions through the Bank of Maldives and the Bank of Ceylon, and did not pass suspected money-laundering cases on. The unit's former head, Ibrahim Athif Shakoor, said governor Azeema Adam objected to filing a police report, citing too few staff and resources; Azeema said she had told him to investigate SOF's transactions and gave no specific instructions because the unit decided its own actions. In March 2019 police summoned governor Ahmed Naseer and confirmed he was being investigated for obstruction of justice, with no charge or court outcome named. He resigned in July 2019 amid allegations that he had got around the authority's rules and interfered in the unit's inquiries, one of them into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election; Naseer denied influencing the unit and made counter-allegations, and no charges or findings followed. In February 2020 the Prosecutor General's Office charged Shakoor with negligence and failing to act appropriately on the case; he denied the allegations, and on 14 October 2025 that office withdrew the charge, citing how long it had been in court, with no conviction reported. One career move is documented: Ali Hashim, who was finance minister under former president Mohamed Nasheed from November 2008 to December 2010 and who also chaired the Addu International Airport Company during the previous MDP government, with no years given for that, was nominated by President Ibrahim Mohamed Solih for the vacant post of governor of the authority, as reported on 29 August 2019. Deloitte Partners in Male' audited the 2024 accounts. On 7 October 2024 India agreed a currency-borrowing line of 400 million US dollars and 30 billion Indian rupees. The authority scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Its notes are printed abroad. De La Rue's launch release says the family of six notes introduced on 1 November 2015, from 10 to 1,000 rufiyaa, was designed by local designer Abdullah Nashaath and printed by De La Rue on polymer, in close association with the Monetary Authority.
p:URY: Uruguay's money is the peso, issued by the Central Bank of Uruguay and held within a moving band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 17 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 43, although the country scores 73 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. One case is recorded, from 2017, and it was dismissed: prosecutor Rodrigo Morosoli, investigating the Cambio Nelson fraud at a currency exchange house, sought the formal indictment of Humberto Capote, a former president of the bank, for taking part in a continuing crime of misappropriation. Judge Marcelo Souto freed Capote at first instance, finding the evidence insufficient to prosecute him, and the prosecutor appealed in April 2017. No government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. The accounts are audited by the Tribunal de Cuentas under the 1995 charter law. The bank is also named among the central bank clients of a fixed-income fund built around environmental and social standards, developed jointly by Amundi and the Latin American Reserve Fund; it invests in that fund rather than handing them its reserves to manage. Three people have moved between the bank and outside jobs. Guillermo Tolosa confirmed in December 2024 that he would preside over the bank once Yamandu Orsi took office as president of Uruguay; he had worked as an economist at the International Monetary Fund and as a consultant at Oxford Economics, and was academic director of the research centre Ceres from 2018 to 2020. Washington Ribeiro spent 15 years on the bank's board, as director from June 2010 to March 2020, vice president from March 2020 to July 2024 and president from July 2024 to March 2025, and on 7 April 2026 he started as head of Uruguayan macro and sovereign strategy at the Uruguayan brokerage Latin Securities. Diego Labat, president of the bank from 2020 to 2024, was named general manager of the Bolsa Electronica de Valores by its board on 20 August 2025, replacing a man who had held the post for 25 years. The exchange was founded in January 1993 by 26 financial institutions operating in Uruguay, both public and private, so how far this is a move into private finance is not clear-cut. Its notes are printed abroad by Oberthur Fiduciaire, which printed the revised 2,000-peso note dated 2015 that the bank introduced on 27 April 2016, carrying a holographic windowed security thread and a map of Uruguay.
n:Grant Thornton DOO: Grant Thornton DOO is an accountancy firm in Skopje, the North Macedonian member of the Grant Thornton international network. It audits the accounts of the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia, which means checking the bank's books from outside and reporting on them. It signed the Independent Auditor's Report on the bank's financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2023, addressed to the bank's Council, and gave an opinion without qualifications. The bank publishes the report on its own website and in the Official Gazette. Grant Thornton is one of the mid-tier networks that sit below the four largest accountancy firms.
n:Fidelity Printers and Refiners: Fidelity Printers and Refiners is a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, based in Harare. It prints the country's banknotes, which means Zimbabwe's money is made by a company the central bank itself owns rather than bought from an outside printer. Its own corporate history says the work began in 1966 in the basement of the old Reserve Bank building on Samora Machel Avenue, and moved to purpose-built premises at Msasa in 1978-82. In 2021 the printing side was split off into a separate company, the Printing and Minting Company of Zimbabwe. A bank that owns its printer is not unusual and is in some ways the opposite of the risk this map tracks elsewhere, where an outside firm holds the contract; what it does mean is that there is no outside party whose contract terms or payments a reader could examine.
n:Banknote Printing Works of the Nationa: The Banknote Printing Works of the National Bank of Cambodia is the central bank's own printing works. It prints the country's banknotes, so the riel is made in-house rather than ordered from one of the handful of commercial printers that supply most of the world. It is recorded here as the printer of the 200,000-riel note issued on 16 October 2024 for the twentieth anniversary of King Norodom Sihamoni's coronation. As with other state works, there is no outside contract to examine, and what is known here comes from a specialist banknote news service rather than from a document the bank itself publishes.
n:RSM Tajikistan LLC: RSM Tajikistan LLC is an accountancy firm in Dushanbe, the Tajik member of the RSM international network. It audits the accounts of the National Bank of Tajikistan, which means checking the bank's books from outside and reporting on them. Its managing partner signed the independent auditor's report on the bank's 2023 financial statements, and the firm holds a licence from the National Bank itself to audit banks, which is worth noticing: the body being audited is also the body that licenses its auditor. RSM is one of the mid-tier networks that sit below the four largest accountancy firms. Earlier audits of this bank were done by Deloitte and by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder; this is the current mandate.
